title: A Lantern for the Compass
premise: In 1913, Ulyana Iversen serves as driver and letter-reader for the Marchmont suffragist household, a found family of servants and activists bound by secrets. When a sealed dispatch reveals that the family's patron has been named in an anarchist bombing plot he did not commit, the state closes in, and the only escape is a single berth on the last river steamer before the ice breaks. Ulyana, who has spent her life invisible, must decide who among them carries the family's future north—and discovers her own name belongs on that list. The novel ends with Ulyana surrendering the berth to the youngest member, staying behind to testify, and finding that justice outside the law begins with refusing to disappear.
about_author: Oscar Nakamura is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing intercepted letters from early twentieth-century political movements. They write historical fiction about the people history files under 'correspondence.'

chapters.title: The Weight of Envelopes
chapters.summary: Ulyana Iversen, the Marchmonts' driver, opens and reads every letter before delivering it—a habit born of protecting the suffragist household from informers. Through her POV we meet the sprawling found family: cook Marta, printer's apprentice Sef, young ward Lidiya. The beat is quiet competence masking loneliness; Ulyana measures her worth in what she can carry for others.

chapters.title: Orders Come in Winter
chapters.summary: A government circular warns of raids on radical households. Ulyana burns three letters and coaches the staff on their stories. POV shifts briefly to Inspector Rell, building his file on the Marchmont circle. The emotional beat is the family rehearsing invisibility like a play they've performed too many times.

chapters.title: What Marta Keeps Under the Floor
chapters.summary: Marta's POV: beneath the kitchen floor lie pamphlets, a pistol, and letters from her executed brother. She and Ulyana share brandy and confessions, deepening their bond. Beat: tenderness between women who trust no one else, and the first hint that Marta's health is failing.

chapters.title: The Sealed One
chapters.summary: A letter arrives sealed in wax Ulyana doesn't recognize—official, not personal. Against every instinct she steams it open: it names Patrik Marchmont as financier of a bombing that killed four people. He didn't do it, but the evidence is tailored. Beat: dread; the world Ulyana managed is now managing her.

chapters.title: Patrik's Denial
chapters.summary: Patrik's POV: he confronts the accusation privately with Ulyana, revealing he was elsewhere that night—with a woman who cannot testify without ruining her own family. His pride wars with terror. Beat: the patriarch becomes mortal; Ulyana realizes she holds his alibi and his ruin in the same hand.

chapters.title: Lidiya Learns to Listen
chapters.summary: Fifteen-year-old Lidiya eavesdrops on the adults' council of war and starts keeping her own coded notebook, imitating Ulyana. Beat: bittersweet—the child is becoming what the family made her, sharp and watchful, and Ulyana both admires and grieves it.

chapters.title: Sef and the Printing Press
chapters.summary: Sef proposes printing Patrik's defense themselves, but the press would prove the raid justified. His POV shows youthful fury at injustice channeled into recklessness. Beat: the family fractures over tactics—fight, flee, or fold—and Ulyana casts the deciding silence.

chapters.title: Inspector Rell's Doubt
chapters.summary: Rell's POV: he examines the case against Marchmont and finds the evidence too neat, likely manufactured by a rival faction within the police. He wants the truth but not enough to burn his career. Beat: the antagonist revealed as a man trapped by the same machinery he serves.

chapters.title: The River Schedule
chapters.summary: Ulyana learns the last steamer north departs when the ice breaks—eleven days—and there is one berth, secured years ago under a false name for exactly this contingency. Whose name goes on it? Beat: hope arrives shaped like an impossible arithmetic problem.

chapters.title: Everyone Argues for Someone Else
chapters.summary: The family meets; each argues another deserves the berth—Marta for Lidiya, Patrik for Marta, Sef for himself then recants. Ulyana watches the poor perform generosity while the rich perform sacrifice. Beat: love exposed as competition, and the first open wound between Ulyana and Patrik.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Cannot Testify
chapters.summary: Ulyana tracks down Patrik's alibi, Elena, and offers to protect her identity if she'll sign a statement. Elena refuses—not from fear but shame. Beat: Ulyana's first real failure; justice requires truths people won't give.

chapters.title: Raid
chapters.summary: The police come at dawn. Ulyana's preparations hold—nothing damning is found—but Marta collapses under the strain and is taken for questioning. Beat: terror rendered procedural; the house that hid everyone can no longer hide itself.

chapters.title: Marta in Custody
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs: Marta enduring interrogation with iron courtesy, and Ulyana bribing a clerk for news. Marta protects the family by claiming sole ownership of the contraband. Beat: fierce gratitude curdling into guilt—someone always pays for someone else's safety.

chapters.title: Rell Offers a Bargain
chapters.summary: Rell privately tells Ulyana he believes Patrik innocent and will bury the file if the family leaves quietly—but the berth means one person only, and Marta's release depends on cooperation. Beat: temptation; the lawful path and the just path diverge visibly for the first time.

chapters.title: What Ulyana Carries
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter: Ulyana's childhood as a stowaway's daughter, how she learned that being carried means being disposable. Her POV returns fully. Beat: the thematic keystone—she has spent her life earning a place by carrying things, and now must claim one by standing still.

chapters.title: Lidiya's Notebook Found
chapters.summary: A second search turns up Lidiya's coded notebook; she is detained as a material witness. The family's careful architecture of protection collapses around its youngest. Beat: rage and helplessness; Ulyana understands the state punishes children for adults' convictions.

chapters.title: The Forged Statement
chapters.summary: Sef forges Elena's signature on the alibi statement; Ulyana must decide whether to deliver a lie that could free two people or destroy them all if detected. She delivers it. Beat: the moral center crosses her own line, choosing people over principle.

chapters.title: Ice Cracking
chapters.summary: The river groans; the steamer loads tomorrow. Marta is released, broken-lunged; Lidiya remains held pending trial. Rell signals that the forged statement worked but he cannot protect them further. Beat: breathless compression—everything converges on one night and one berth.

chapters.title: The Last Berth
chapters.summary: Climax part one: at the dock, Ulyana puts Lidiya's name on the ticket, smuggles her from custody via the clerk she bribed, and puts her on the boat. Patrik protests; Ulyana overrules him with the authority of the invisible. Beat: triumphant heartbreak—the family's future leaves without its architect.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Climax part two: instead of fleeing, Ulyana walks into the courthouse and testifies openly—her reading of letters, the forged statement, the manufactured evidence—burning her own invisibility as fuel. Rell corroborates. Beat: catharsis through exposure; justice begins where secrecy ends.

chapters.title: Verdicts
chapters.summary: Patrik is cleared; Ulyana receives a suspended sentence and loses everything employable about her old life. Marta dies gently that spring, asking Ulyana to read her one last letter—blank paper, so Ulyana writes it herself. Beat: grief braided with vindication.

chapters.title: A Lantern for the Compass
chapters.summary: Epilogue: Lidiya writes from the north; Ulyana, unemployable and finally visible, opens a small courier service that delivers letters honestly—reading none of them unless asked. The found family persists in correspondence. Final beat: she no longer measures herself in what she carries, but in what she returns.
